body.p: This responds to the Final Office Action dated November 21, 2024.
Claims 1-6, 13-16, and 21-22 are presently amended. Claims 11 and 19 were canceled
previously. Claims 21-22 are withdrawn. No new claim is added. As a result, claims 1-10, 12-18, and 20-22 are now pending in this application.
Applicant respectfully submits that no new matter has been introduced, and that the
amendment is supported by, for example, [0075]-[0078] and FIG. 4 of the Application as filed.
Applicant thanks Examiner Eric Messersmith for the courtesy of a helpful telephone

interview on January 9, 2025, with Applicant's representative Dan Li, during which the Restriction Requirement, the rejections of claim 1 under § § 101 and 102, and distinctions between the claimed subject matter and the cited art (Colman) were discussed. The Examiner was provided with an Interview Agenda, in which Applicant's representative proposed amending claim 1 to incorporate the cardiorespiratory event detector from claim 2, and further to require the first signal metric be generated using respiration information and the second or the third signal metric be generated using heart sound information (proposal 1), or sampling of measurements of the second signal metric only when the third signal metric satisfies a specific condition (proposal 2). The Examiner indicated that incorporating claim 2 into claim 1 would appear to overcome the 101 rejection, and amendment proposals 1 and 2 would appear to overcome the current art rejection subject to further consideration and supplemental search in view of a formal response.

Claims 1 and 13 were objected to because of the following informalities: In the penultimate line of each claim, "pulmonary risk" should be changed to "pulmonary risk score." Applicant has amended said claims accordingly, and respectfully requests withdrawal such objection.
Claim 3 was objected to because of the following informalities: In line 5 of the claim, it

appears that "based at in part" should be changed to "based at least in part." Applicant has amended said claim accordingly. Similar amendment was also made to claims 15 and 22. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal such objection.

The Office Action asserts that claims 21-22 are directed to an invention that is independent or distinct from the invention originally claimed, and restricts the claims to one of the following under 35 U.S.C. 121:
I. Claims 1-10 and 12, drawn to a medical device system for calculating and providing
a pulmonary risk score, classified in 600/529.
II. Claims 13-18, drawn to a method of calculating and providing a pulmonary risk
score, classified in 600/529.
III. Claims 21-22, drawn to a medical device system for calculating a pulmonary risk
score and detecting a cardiorespiratory risk, classified in 600/484.
Applicant provisionally elects, with traverse, Group I, claims 1-10 and 12.

The Office Action asserts that "invention I and III ... have a materially different effect in that no specific event is determined in Invention I. In addition, there is nothing that is output in invention III. Furthermore, the inventions as claimed do not encompass overlapping subject matter and there is nothing of record to show them to be obvious variants. Since applicant has received an action on the merits for the originally presented invention, this invention has been constructively elected by original presentation for prosecution on the merits. Accordingly, claims 21-22 are withdrawn from consideration as being directed to a non-elected invention. See 37 CFR 1.142(b) and MPEP § 821.03." (Office Action 2-3.)

As Applicant explained in the Response dated August 12, 2024, claim 21 incorporates the limitations of original claim 1 (except for the "output circuit") and original claim 2, and the requirement of the primary pulmonary risk score and the secondary pulmonary risk score each taking a numerical value, as similarly made to claim 1. The Office Action asserts that "no specific event is determined in Invention I." Claim 2 of Invention I, however, explicitly recites a physiological event detector circuit configured to automatically detect a cardiorespiratory event, a limitation similarly recited in claim 21. The Office Action further asserts that "the inventions [I and III] as claimed do not encompass overlapping subject matter." Claim 1 (of Invention I) and claim 21 (of Invention III) both recite a risk stratification circuit performing substantially identical functions.
Furthermore, although claim 21 does not explicitly recite an "output circuit" (as recited in

claim 1), claim 21 recites a physiological event detector circuit to detect a cardiorespiratory event of the patient based at least in part on the calculated composite pulmonary risk score. This suggests that the calculated composite pulmonary risk score is output to the physiological event detector circuit, which then detects a cardiorespiratory event based on said risk score. Detecting a cardiorespiratory event is clearly a variant of "providing the calculated composite pulmonary risk score to a user or a process," as required by claim 1.

Finally, because original claims 1 and 2 have both been examined on the merit, and claim 21 incorporates the limitations of original claim 1 (except for the "output circuit") and original claim 2, no serious burden of search and examination is believed required.
For at least the foregoing reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that the restriction between Inventions I and III is improper.

Additionally, Applicant has amended claim 1 to incorporate the limitation from claim 2. As such, claim 1 of Group I and claim 21 of Group III both require a physiological event detector circuit configured to detect a cardiorespiratory event of the patient based at least in part on the calculated composite pulmonary risk score. Claim 13 of Group II has been amended similarly to recite automatically detecting, via a physiological event detector circuit, a cardiorespiratory event of the patient based at least in part on the calculated composite pulmonary risk score. In view of such amendment, the asserted basis of restriction no longer applies; and no serious search and examination burden appears required. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests coherent, efficient, and expeditious examination of claims 1-10, 12-18, and 20-22.

To the extent that the provisionally non-elected claims are deemed withdrawn by the Office, Applicant reserves the right to request rejoinder or to reintroduce such provisionally non-elected claims later during prosecution in the present application, or to present the non-elected claims in one or more continuation or divisional applications at a later date.
The Rejection of Claims Under ? 101
Claims 1, 5-6, 8-13 and 16-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as allegedly being directed to non-statutory subject matter.
The Office Action asserts that said claims are directed to an abstract idea without

significantly more, and that the claims recite the process of using a mathematical formula to output a pulmonary risk score. (Office Action at 4.) Without acquiescing to such assertions, Applicant has amended claim 1, among other things, to incorporate the limitation of original claim 2 ("a physiological event detector circuit configured to detect a cardiorespiratory event of the patient based at least in part on the calculated composite pulmonary risk score.") Claim 2 was not rejected on the ineligibility basis. Detecting a cardiorespiratory event based on the pulmonary risk score amounts to significantly more than the alleged judicial exception (mathematical formula to compute a pulmonary risk score), such that it is integrated into a practical application.

Applicant further submits that claim 1 is patent eligible in view of Federal Circuit's decision on CardioNet, LLC v. InfoBionic, Inc., No. 19-1149 (Fed. Cir. 2020). Claim 1 of CardioNet, reproduced below, is directed to a device to detect an event relevant to atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter based on variability in the beat-to-beat timing.
1. A device, comprising:

a beat detector to identify a beat-to-beat timing of cardiac activity; a ventricular beat detector to identify ventricular beats in the cardiac activity; variability determination logic to determine a variability in the beat-to-beat timing of a collection of beats;
relevance determination logic to identify a relevance of the variability in the beat-to-beat timing to at least one of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter; and
an event generator to generate an event when the variability in the beat-to- beat timing is identified as relevant to the at least one of atrial fibrillation and atrial
flutter in light of the variability in the beat-to-beat timing caused by ventricular beats
identified by the ventricular beat detector.

The Federal Circuit held that, when read as a whole and in light of the written description, claims directed to an improvement in cardiac monitoring technology are not directed to an abstract idea. See id. at p. 13. Similar to the "event generator" of the CardioNet claim that generates an event of atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter based on variability in the beat-to-beat timing, Applicant's claim 1 recites a "physiological event detector" to detect a cardiorespiratory event based on the calculated composite pulmonary risk score. With respect to the disclosures, similar to CardioNet patent's disclosure that the claimed invention achieves more accurate and clinically significant detection of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter which constitutes an improvement to cardiac monitoring technology, Applicant's disclosure describes improved cardiorespiratory event detection guided by

the composite pulmonary risk score, including more timely detection with increased accuracy (e.g., lower false positive detections). For example, as described in Applicant's specification, pulmonary disease detection may be turned off or temporarily withhold if the patient has a low pulmonary risk, and turned back on when the patient has a high pulmonary risk. (See Application at [0095] and FIG. 6.) Table 1 further shows examples of various cardiorespiratory event detection algorithms corresponding to different pulmonary risk levels. Accordingly, a more accurate composite pulmonary risk assessment, such as in accordance with the claimed invention, would lead to improved accuracy of risk-based cardiorespiratory event detection. Furthermore, using the pulmonary risk assessment as described in Applicant's specification can help save battery power and conserve computing resources, thereby improving the functionality of the medical-device system.

Because Applicant's claim 1 includes similar limitations to those of the eligible claim 1 of CardioNet, said claim is submitted to be patent-eligible for similar reasons set forth in the CardioNet decision.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of such rejection and allowance of claims 1, 5-6, 8-13 and 16-20.
The Rejection of Claims Under ? 102
Claims 1-2, 4, 12-14 and 20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a) over Colman (U.S. 2011/0040713). Applicant respectfully traverses.

Applicant has amended claim 1 to more distinctly recite certain aspects of the present subject matter, including, among other things, a risk stratification circuit configured to receive physiological information including respiration information and heart sound information sensed from a patient, and generate distinct first, second, and third signal metrics using the received physiological information, the first signal metric generated using the received respiration information, the second or the third signal metric generated using the received heart sound information, and a physiological event detector circuit configured to detect a cardiorespiratory event of the patient based at least in part on the calculated composite pulmonary risk score.
Colman mentions various signal metrics being used for generating a pulmonary index
output, but is silent on a first signal metric generated using respiration information, the second or the third signal metric generated using heart sound information, as required by claim 1. Because
Colman fails to disclose each and every claim limitation in claim 1, a primafacie case of anticipation has not been established with respect to claim 1.
Claim 13 has been similarly amended claim 1, and is submitted to be patentable for the same reason set forth above with respect to claim 1.

Claims 2, 4, and 12 are dependent from base claim 1. Claims 14 and 20 are dependent form base claim 13. Such dependent claims each include patentable subject matter beyond that recited in their respective base claims, and are believed to be patentable for at least the reasons stated above with respect to the respective base claims.
Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of this basis of rejection and allowance of claims 1-2, 4, 12-14 and 20.
The Rejection of Claims Under ? 103

Claims 3, 8-10, 15 and 17-18 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Colman in view of An (U.S. 2013/0116578); Claim 5 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Colman in view of Patangay (U.S. 2012/0157799); Claims 6-7 and 16 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over Colman in view of Dumont (U.S. 2014/0243690).
Applicant respectfully traverses the above rejections under § 103. The combination of

Colman with any of An, Patangay, or Dumont, as suggested in the Office Action, does not rectify the deficiency of Colman, as stated above with respect to claims 1 and 13, such that a primafacie case of obviousness has not been established with respect to said claims because all claimed features have not been disclosed or suggested by the combined references.
Furthermore, regarding claims 6 and 16 (which have been amended to clarify that the

measurements of the second signal metric used for the calculating the secondary pulmonary risk score are sampled only at times when the third signal metric satisfies a specified condition), the Office Action relies on Dumont to teach such "conditional sampling" feature. Dumon refers to a decision tree that employs activity V1 and average respiratory frequency V2 to decide whether to issue an alert or not. (FIG. 1 and [0058]-[0063].) Dumon, however, does not teach or suggest sampling measurements of one signal metric (e.g., respiratory frequency data V2) only at times when another signal metric (e.g., activity V1) satisfies a specific condition. Checking the activity V1 against a specific condition (above or below the threshold T1, e.g., 1 hr/day) is merely used for

setting different thresholds (T2 or T3) for the respiratory frequency data V2. Dumon is silent on using activity V1 satisfying a specific condition to trigger or gate sampling of respiratory frequency data V2. Instead, the activity V1 and respiratory frequency V2 data appear to be independently collected and applied to the decision tree that logically decides whether to issue an alert or not. Nothing in Dumon teaches or suggests that the comparison of the activity to the threshold T1 would affect the sampling of respiratory frequency data.

For at least the foregoing reasons, Dumon fails to rectify the deficiency of Colman, such that aprimafacie case of obviousness has not been established with respect to each of claims 6 and 16. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration, withdrawal of this basis of rejection, and allowance of claims 6-7 and 16.
Previously withdrawn claim 21 has been amended to include such "conditionalsampling"

features similar to claim 6 (calculating a secondary pulmonary risk score using measurements of the second signal metric sampled only at times when the third signal metric satisfies a specific condition). For at least the same reasons set forth above with respect to claim 6, Applicant respectfully submits that claim 21 is patentable over Colman in view of Dumont.

In the interest of clarity and brevity, every assertion made in the Office Action may not have been equally addressed. Silence regarding any such assertion does not constitute any admission or acquiescence. All rights not exercised in connection with this response, such as the right to challenge or rebut any tacit or explicit characterization of any reference or of any of the present claims, the right to challenge or rebut any asserted factual or legal basis of any of the rejections, the right to swear behind any cited reference such as provided under 37 C.F.R. § 1.131 or otherwise, or the right to assert co-ownership of any cited reference, are reserved. It is not admitted that any of the cited references or any other references of record are relevant to the present claims, or that they constitute prior art. To the extent that any rejection or assertion is based upon the Examiner's personal knowledge, rather than any objective evidence of record as manifested by a cited prior art reference, timely objection to such reliance on Official Notice is made, and all rights to request that the Examiner provide a reference or affidavit in support of such assertion, as required by MPEP § 2144.03, are reserved. All rights to pursue any cancelled claims in a subsequent patent application
claiming the benefit of priority of the present patent application, and to request rejoinder of any
withdrawn claim, as required by MPEP § 821.04, are likewise reserved.

It is respectfully submitted that the claims are in condition for allowance, and notification to that effect is earnestly requested. The Examiner is invited to telephone the undersigned at (612) 373- 6900 to facilitate prosecution of this application.
If necessary, please charge any additional fees or deficiencies, or credit any overpayments to Deposit Account No. 19-0743.
